title: How Wet Nurses Survived Selling Their Milk to the Rich
fullText: In the center of ancient Rome near the theater of Marcelus, there stood a stone column called the columna Lactaria, the milk column. According to the Roman Grimarian Fesus, it was so-called because they would bring babies there to be fed with milk. Women gathered around that column to sell their breast milk to strangers. They nursed abandoned infants. They offered their services to wealthy families who could afford to pay. That was roughly 2,000 years ago. And the astonishing part is what happened next, which is basically nothing. The women kept showing up. Century after century, empire after empire, the same spot in Rome, served as an open air hiring hall for wet nurses. The column eventually disappeared, but the square it stood on, the Piaza Montinara, kept doing exactly the same job. Women still gathered there to sell their milk as late as 1,928. When Mussolini demolished the piaza to build a road that was 1,928 nearly 2,000 years after the column Lactaria was first erected, the trade it hosted was still running. So what exactly was wet nursing? Who were the women selling their milk? And why were so many families buying it? And how did this one profession manage to survive every plague, every revolution, every war, and every shift in medical thinking for close to 4,000 years? The answers start in the desert on a 7 1/2 ft slab of black stone. Babylon 1,754 B.CE. The code of Hammurabi is one of the oldest surviving legal codes on Earth. carved onto a diorite stellar that now sits in the Louvre. It covers everything from property disputes to trade agreements to assault and buried in it is law 194 which deals specifically with wet nurses. The law says that if a man gives his son to a wet nurse and that son dies in her care and the nurse then secretly takes on another child without telling the dead infant's parents, she is to be prosecuted. The punishment was that her breasts would be cut off. I mean, think about that for a second. Nearly 4,000 years ago, the profession of wet nursing was already so established, so regulated, and so fraught with potential abuse that the king of Babylon wrote a specific law about it. And the penalty targeted the very body part that made the crime possible. The Acadian word for wet nurse was mushikum, meaning the one who suckles. She was a licensed professional. Sumerian and old Babylonian baby suckling contracts called Gigga laid out terms of 2 to three years of service. The nurse received rations of oil, barley, and wool. A standard fee was about three shekels of silver per year. This was not informal child care. This was a regulated labor market with written contracts and criminal penalties. And Babylon was not alone. In ancient Egypt, the royal wet nurse held a title, Menat Nzut. And unlike most women in the ancient world, she could rise to extraordinary status. Her sons bore the title of milk brother of the king and could enter the highest offices in the land. Consider Citra Inn, the wet nurse of the pharaoh hatchepoot around 1,490 B.CE. Citra Inn was buried in KV60, a tomb in the Valley of the Kings, the most sacred burial ground in Egypt. Howard Carter discovered her mummy in 1903. Her life-sized statue in the Cairo Museum shows her holding the young queen on her lap, a wet nurse buried among pharaohs. Or Maya, the wet nurse of Tutin Carmon around 1,340 B.CE. Her rock cut tomb at Sakara was discovered by the French Egyptologist Alan Zevi in 1996 and opened to the public in 2015. The reliefs carved into the walls show the boy king sitting on her lap surrounded by adoring officials. Zivi has even proposed controversially that Maya may have been Tuten Carmon's own elder sister Mary Tartan. These women were not servants. They were quasi royalty, honored for the specific act of feeding a king from their own body. By the time we reach ancient Greece and Rome, the profession had spread across the entire Mediterranean. Greek nurses were called tit or trophus. Spartan wet nurses were the most prized in the Greek world. Plutarch noted that even Alibabiades, the famous Athenian general and troublemaker, had a Spartan wet nurse named Amikla. Spartan nurses raised infants without swaddling and were so valued for their toughness that they were exported across Greece like a luxury good. The most famous wet nurse in all of Western literature is Urica. She appears in Homer's Odyssey. Leertes bought her for 20 oxen. And when Odysius returns home after 20 years disguised as a beggar, it is Uraclea who recognizes him. She is washing his feet and her hand passes over the scar on his thigh from a childhood boar hunt. The bowl crashes to the floor. She knows. He grabs her by the throat to keep her silent. Her name means wide fame. And Homer gave that name to a wet nurse. In Rome, the profession was enormous. Soranis of Ephesus writing around 100 CE produced a set of criteria for selecting a wet nurse that would dominate European medical thinking for the next 1500 years. The ideal nurse should be between 20 and 40. Should have already borne two or three children. Should be of large frame and good color with medium-sized soft breasts. She should be self-controlled, sympathetic, not illtempered and tidy. Saranus even invented the fingernail test. You placed a drop of the nurse's milk on your thumbnail and tilted your hand. If the drop held its shape, the milk was good. Not everyone approved. The stoic philosopher Favinus, preserved in the writings of Orleskelas, railed against the entire practice. He asked what the reason could possibly be for corrupting a newborn's body and mind with the alien and degenerate nourishment of another's milk. He was especially disgusted when the nurse was a slave or a foreigner. He called wet nursing half motherhood. The Roman historian Tacitus went further. He blamed the moral decline of Rome itself on the replacement of proper Roman matrons with what he called grecul and little Greek slave girls nursing Rome's children. and around 46 wet nursing contracts survive on papyrie from Greco Roman Egypt stretching from 231 B.CE through the Roman period. In one dated 13 B.CEE a nurse named Diddima is hired to feed a foundling. She swears not to sleep with a man, become pregnant, or suckle another child for the duration of the contract. In another, a nurse named Senosirus receives 12 silver drame per year, plus monthly wheat, oil, annual clothing, and two patchwork blankets. 31 of 38 identifiable Roman period contracts involve slave infants. Many of them foundlings described with the formula raised up from the dung heap. This is not a footnote in ancient history. This was one of the largest female labor markets in the preodern world, spanning civilizations and millennia with laws, contracts, medical textbooks, and gravestones. To prove it, Roman tombstones commemorate hundreds of nurses. The Latin title conlé, meaning milk siblings, shows that the children of the nurse and the children she nursed were considered kin. And the same obsessive logic that drove Sarannis to write his selection criteria, the belief that a nurse's milk carried her character, her morals, her intelligence, and her temperament directly into the child, would eventually build one of the most elaborate and deadly systems of infant displacement in European history. The same theory that told wealthy mothers they were protecting their babies by hiring the perfect nurse was about to start killing those babies by the thousands. To understand how breast milk became big business, you have to understand what doctors actually believed milk was. For most of recorded western medical history from antiquity through the 1700s, the dominant theory of the human body was galenic hummeral medicine, four humors, blood, flem, yellow bile, black bile. Every person's temperament, intelligence, morality, and physical constitution was supposedly determined by the balance of these fluids. And breast milk according to Galen and every physician who followed him for 15 centuries was twice cooked menstrual blood. Literally the body took menstrual blood refined it twice and produced milk which meant the milk carried everything. The nurse's personality, her temper, her courage, her laziness, her morals. All of it supposedly seeped directly into the nursing infant through her breast. The 16th century English physician Thomas Muffett put it bluntly. He wrote that no man could doubt that a child's mind was answerable to his nurses milk and manners. His proof Jupiter and Agisus were leerous because they were fed goats milk. Romulus and Polyphimas were cruel because they were nursed by she wolves. Michelangelo himself reportedly claimed through the biographer Vasari that he had absorbed his talent with a chisel from his wet nurse who happened to be the daughter of a stonemason. The Roman historian Suatonius wrote that the emperor Caligula's wet nurse used to smear blood on her nipples to quiet the infant. Later writers pointed to this as proof of his future bloodlust as if the violence had entered him through the milk. This belief system turned the hiring of a wet nurse into something closer to breeding livestock. The selection manuals read like it. Nurses must not be Jewish or Muslim lest the child receive the blood of an infidel. Must not be red-haired, which was considered a mark of ill temper. Must not be pregnant, menrating or pockmarked. Soranis' criteria from the second century. The trotula medical texts from 12th century Seno. Paulo Bagelardo's handbook printed in Padua in 1472, the first pediatrics book ever published. They all say essentially the same thing. Pick the nurse the way you'd pick a mare. And there was one rule above all others. Galen taught that sex spoiled the milk and that a new pregnancy would corrupt it completely. This single belief became the structural foundation of the entire wet nursing economy. Because if the nurse couldn't have sex, someone had to enforce that. The historian Christian Clapish Zuba demonstrated in her landmark study of Renaissance Florence that wet nurse contracts were drawn between two men, the father of the wealthy child and the husband of the wet nurse. Rich men were essentially paying poor men to give up sexual access to their wives so those wives could feed wealthy infants while the wealthy wives got back to making more heirs. In 1395 in Dartington, England, a wet nurse named Isabelle was hired to feed the heir John Deholand. Her husband John Hugh left Dartington for Gernzi because De Holland forbade him from having marital relations with Isabel for three full years. This is where the demand side and the supply side of the milk economy locked together. Because breastfeeding suppresses ovulation, a nursing mother typically cannot conceive for months or even years. So by handing the baby to a wet nurse, the wealthy mother's body reset almost immediately. She could be pregnant again within weeks. For royal courts, this was not a convenience. It was a reproductive strategy. The wives of Philip II of Spain, Katherine Demed Meddichi, and the Bourban Queens all used wet nurses specifically to maintain what one historian called rapid reproductive cadences. Air after air after air. And on the other side of that equation stood the women who actually supplied the milk, rural peasant women mostly. In 18th and 19th century France, the Morvin region of Burgundy became so dependent on the wet nursing trade that its population swelled by 35,000. In Spain, foundling hospitals called inclusers each maintained registries of over a thousand external nurses. Berieved mothers whose own babies had died offered their milk because the alternative was to let it dry up and lose the income entirely. In one 15th century case from Zaragoza, a woman named Maria Garces, having lost her own son, nursed an abandoned newborn for three years. Widows and unmarried mothers turned to wet nursing because it was one of the few respectable wages available to a single woman. In Marles's hospital records, only 43% of contracted nurses were even identified by reference to a husband. And then there was what the historian Valerie Fes called the cascading of milk. Urban poor mothers would farm their own babies out to even poorer rural women at a lower rate so they could nurse a wealthier family's child at a higher one. Filders summarized the arrangement with a line that's hard to forget. She wrote that wealthy parents frequently bought the life of their infant for the life of another. The wages tell the story. In medieval Marseilles, archival work by Kaye McCarthy traced wet nurse pay at the hospital duispris from 1306 to 1457. Wages climbed slowly for decades. Four su a month in 1306, five sus by 1330. Then the black death hit. In 1348, wages exploded to over 26 sus. By 1409, they reached 64 su a month, a 433% jump in a single year after the plague. Because so many nurses had died that the survivors could name their price. The provinile government tried to cap wet nurse pay at six leaves a year, the hospital paid double. Private families paid even more. In 1328, a woman named Sibilia Dragon paid her nurse 110 SUS per year, nearly twice the hospital rate. Most people never heard about what this system looked like at full scale. And the place that built the biggest version of it was Paris. The Parisian wet nursing business was the largest, most bureaucratized infant displacement system in European history. By the medieval period, licensed female brokers called recommendases matched country nurses to urban families. Formal royal regulation came in 1715. The bureau deurisses was placed under the left tenant general of police in 1769 and survived until 1876. The mechanics were staggering. Licensed brokers monopolized the supply of nurses. Carriers called manurs physically transported nursing age infants in carts and pias sometimes 50 to 150 miles from Paris to villages in the Morvan, Bovveses, Picardi and Normandy. They carried back wages, packages, and surviving toddlers 2 to four years later. The most dramatic number comes from a 1,780 report by Lieutenant General Jean Sha Pierre Lenoir. Of 21,000 babies born in Paris that year, only about 1,000 were nursed by their own mothers. Around 1,500 had livein wet nurses at home. The remaining 19,000 were sent to the countryside. 19,000 babies loaded into carts shipped out of Paris to be fed by strangers. The historian Dominique Rizzler observed that all Paris with the exception of nobility and beggars participates in this migration of newborns towards the pure air of the country of 66,259 nursings placed through the bureau between 1,770 and 1,776. 31% died in the nurse's care. And that was the regulated system. The better outcome. Foundling mortality in the Burbanet reached 80% in Maine 75. Paris and Lion earned the nickname Vils Sans Bees, cities without babies. In Florence, the system left an even more detailed paper trail thanks to the Ricardans, the meticulous family memorandum books kept by merchants and nobles. The wool merchant Giovani Morelli writing in the early 1400s recorded his lifelong grief at being sent to a wet nurse as an infant. Lorenzo Demdichi's son Pierro was placed with a Balia in the Mugello Hills. Clapish Zuber discovered that in roughly a quarter of Florentine contracts, only the wet nurse's husband is named. The nurse herself goes unrecorded. She did the work. He signed the paper. The Ospedale Degli Innocenti designed by Brunoleski and funded by the Silk Guild opened its doors on the 5th of February 1,445. It was Europe's first purpose-built foundling hospital. The very first child received that day was named Agata Smeralda. She was dispatched within days to a country wet nurse at Castell Furentino. Babies arrived through a revolving wheel built into the wall beneath a statue of the Madonna. Death rates among the innocent hovered around 30% in normal years and exceeded 50 to 67% during plague years and wet nurse shortages. Over five centuries, the innocent cared for an estimated 375,000 children, the unregulated countryside, the staggering mortality, the brokers and the carts, and the anonymous contracts. All of it was a warning sign. And for centuries, nobody acted on it. Up to this point, the wet nursing system had been driven by economics, bad medicine, and the reproductive math of aristocratic families. That was about to flip because in the American South, the milk was not bought and sold on a contract. It was taken by force from women who had no right to refuse. The key scholarship on enslaved wet nursing in America comes from Emily West and RJ Knight, writing in the Journal of Southern History in 2017 and from Stephanie E. Jones Rogers in her 2019 book, They Were Her Property, Western Knight, estimate that roughly 70,000 enslaved women worked as wet nurses across the antibbellum South. Jones Rogers found over 1,300 wet nurse advertisements in 57 southern newspapers published between 1,800 and 1,865. The language in those ads tells you everything you need to know about how the system worked from the Charleston Mercury the 7th of June 1865. Offer at private sale. A young and healthy wet nurse. From an ad posted on Bofain Street in 1795. A healthy black wet nurse without a child. Without a child, meaning her baby had either died or been sold away from her, so her milk was wholly available for a white infant. From a Charleston ad in November of 1800, a woman who used to attending in the house would answer as a wet nurse in a few weeks. She was being sold while still pregnant. Her future milk, the milk her body had not yet produced for a child she had not yet delivered, was already a commodity on the market. And this is the part where things stopped being funny because we have the voices of the women this happened to. The most direct testimony comes from the WPA slave narratives collected between 1,936 and 1,938 from elderly men and women who had lived through slavery as children. Their words are recorded in dialect by the interviewers, most of whom were white southerners. The quotations are widely accepted by historians, but carry methodological caveats about the conditions under which they were given. What the testimonies describe is not ambiguous. William McWater of Georgia told interviewers about his aunt Mary who belonged to a man named Mars John Kredock. When Kredock's wife died and left a baby girl, little Miss Lucy, Aunt Mary was already nursing a newborn of her own. So Kredock forced her to nurse both. And if Aunt Mary was feeding her own baby when Miss Lucy started crying, Kraock would snatch her baby up by the legs and spank him and tell Aunt Mary to nurse his baby first. Mcuarter said his mother often saw Aunt Mary cry until the tears met under her chin. Mary Jane Jones of Arkansas described a system even more deliberate. She said her mother was given to her master at the time of his marriage as a kind of nest egg to breed slaves for him. Her mother would have a baby every time the mistress had one so that her mother was always available as the wet nurse for the mistress's children. The synchronization was not accidental. Masters either assaulted enslaved women themselves or forced them into sexual relationships with enslaved men, specifically to keep them lactating on the same schedule as white mistresses. What comes next is the part that still doesn't make sense to most people hearing it for the first time. Harriet Jacobs in her 1861 autobiography, Incidents in the Life of a Slave Girl, described a scene she witnessed. A woman ran wildly past her, pursued by two men. She was a slave, the wet nurse of her mistress's children. For some minor offense, her mistress ordered her stripped and whipped. To escape the degradation and the torture, she ran to the river, jumped in, and drowned. Jacobs also recorded that her own mother had been weaned at 3 months old so that the mistress's baby could have more milk. Charity Bowery, interviewed in 1848, said her mother had suckled all of her master's children. And as a reward, the mistress made it a practice to give one of her mother's children to each of the white children she had nursed. Every baby the wet nurse bore became a gift for the white child who had fed at her breast. A pattern called the one breast rule appears across multiple testimonies. Enslaved women were ordered to give one breast to the white baby and reserve the other for their own child, but always to feed the white infant first. The hierarchy was literal, physical, and enforced. The white families who benefited from this system recorded it too, though with a tone that makes the cruelty even harder to stomach. Ella Gertrude Clanton Thomas of Georgia wrote in her diary in 1861 that on Sunday they went down to the Ral plantation for a woman named America. America had lost her baby, which would have been 3 weeks old had it lived. Thomas's father had kindly permitted them to have her as a wet nurse. Thomas cycled through enslaved nurses across her children's infies, America, Georgiana, Emiline, Nancy. She expressed no compassion for America's dead child. She recorded the acquisition of a grieving mother the way someone might note picking up a piece of furniture. Philip Vickers Fythian, a tutor working in Virginia in 1773, wrote in his journal that he found it common for people of fortune to have their young children suckled by enslaved women. He noted it the way you'd note a local custom. Interesting, perhaps, not disturbing. Ellen Craig's mother, years after slavery ended, confronted the white man she had once nursed as an infant. She told him she was going to kill him. "These black titties sucked you," she said. "And then you come out here to beat me." If this history is new to you and you want to understand how deep it runs, subscribe. We cover stories like this every week, the ones that got left out of the textbook. Enter Cassia Roth and the Brazilian archive. Because the American South was not the only slave society that ran on stolen breast milk, Brazil received roughly 5 million enslaved Africans and was the last country in the Western Hemisphere to abolish slavery. On the 13th of May 1888, the wet nursing trade there was enormous. Roth's research uncovered approximately 120,000 individual wet nurse entries in a single newspaper, the journal do Commercio in Rio de Janeiro across the 19th century. The ads read like the Charleston ones from the newspaper O Merkantil on the 30th of April 1845. For rent an 18-year-old girl, wet nurse, healthy and with much good milk for the last 2 months. She is for rent because her child has died. For rent because her child has died. In 1871, Brazil passed the lay du vontra leave the free womb law which declared that all future children born to enslaved women would be free. It sounds like progress. It was the opposite. Because slaveholders no longer had a financial stake in keeping those newborns alive, they had every incentive to separate mother from child as quickly as possible and rent the mother's milk out. Abandonment of newborns surged. A medical student named Juvenile Martino Das Neves described what happened in 1873. The mother would fall asleep after childbirth. While she slept, her baby was taken and sent to the rotor, the foundling wheel. When she woke and looked for her child and learned what had been done, she came undone in tears. One of the few enslaved Brazilian wet nurses whose name and photograph survive is Monica. She nursed Agusto Gomes Le and Isabel Adelaide Le Fernandez in 1860s Pernambuko. In 1912, the painter Lucilio de Albuquerque created a painting called May Pria, Black Mother, showing a melancholy enslaved woman nursing a white infant while her own black baby lies on the ground waiting his turn. The Brazilian abolitionist statesman Wim Nabuko, born in 1849, credited his anonymous May Pria from the Masangana plantation with shaping his moral universe. He never recorded her name. You'd think that after slavery ended, after the economics shifted, after the moral arguments won, that the broader wet nursing system would have cleaned itself up. For a while, things in Victorian England actually seemed respectable. Women advertised their services. Families hired nurses through proper channels. The system looked regulated. That didn't last. In Victorian England, the line between wet nursing and baby farming was almost invisible. A woman could advertise to nurse an infant or to adopt one or simply to take one off your hands for a fee. The British Medical Journal in 1868 called the far end of that spectrum commercial infanticide, and they were not exaggerating. Margaret Waters was a widow operating out of four Frederick Terrace in Brixham. She placed ads offering to adopt infants for fees between 2 and £10. In June of 1870, a police sergeant named Richard Ralph raided her house and found 11 babies. They were emaciated. They were drugged with lordinum. Five of them died shortly after. The case that sent her to the gallows was the death of John Walter Cowan, the illegitimate son of a 17-year-old named Janet Tassie Cowan. The Times called it ruthless and systematic murder. On the 11th of October 1870, Margaret Waters became the first woman executed for baby farming in England. Investigators believe she was responsible for at least 19 deaths. And then Amelia Dyier made the one decision that changed everything about how England policed infant care. Dier operated for nearly 30 years. She is sometimes called the ogress of reading. Victim estimates range from a dozen confirmed kills to over 400, which would make her one of the most prolific serial killers in British history. Her method was simple. She advertised in newspapers as a married couple with no family willing to adopt a healthy child. Nice country home. Terms £10. Mothers, often unmarried women desperate to place their babies, would hand over the child and the fee. Dier would strangle the infant, usually with white edging tape, and dispose of the body. Her undoing came on the 30th of March, 1896, when a bargeman on the tempames at Cavasham fished a brown paper parcel from the water. Inside was the body of a baby girl named Helena Fry, strangled with white tape. The investigation led to Dier. She had taken 3-month-old Doris Marman from a Chelinham barmaid named Eveina Marman and strangled her on March 31. The next day, she killed 13-month-old Harry Simmons. When police confronted her, Dier told them, "You'll know all mine by the tape around their necks." The jury convicted her in 4 and 1/2 minutes. Dier was not alone. Francis Cannor was hanged in Melbourne in January of 1894 after three infant bodies were dug up in her Brunswick gardens. Her hangman killed himself rather than carry out the execution. Mini Dean, the only woman ever judicially executed in New Zealand, was hanged in 1895 for killing infants at a property called the Larches near Winton. Vendors outside her courthouse sold toy dolls in miniature hat boxes. In Sydney in 1893, police found 13 infant corpses buried in the yards of John and Sarah Makin. And in 1903, Amelia Sack and Annie Walters were hanged together at Holay Prison, the last double female hanging in modern British history. Sack ran a lying in home in Finchley. Walters poisoned the babies with chlorodine. The 19th century French had a word for nurses who deliberately let infants die. Fesuses don Angel makers. The lexographer Emil Litter defined the term in 1877 as a nurse who deliberately allows the infants entrusted to her to die. You'd think someone would have said something. Nobody did. Not for decades. Because the infrastructure for keeping babies quiet and keeping questions away was enormous. Godfreyy's cordial, a mixture of lordinum and trile, was the early 19th century standard. One Manchester drugist admitted to selling half a gallon per week. But the real giant was Ms. Winslow's soothing syrup developed by Jeremiah Curtis of Bang, Main starting in 1849. It contained 65 mg of morphine per flu ounce. Curtis testified in 1868 that he was selling 1 and a half million bottles per year. The American Medical Association formally branded it a baby killer in 1911. Other patent narcotics on the market included Atkinson's Royal Infants Preservative, Streets Infant's Quietness, Hodgson's Infant's Preservative, and Steman's Soothing Powders. The physician Thomas Bull estimated in 1854 that 3/4 of all opium deaths in England occurred in children under five. 1 and a half million bottles a year. 65 mg of morphine per ounce sold over the counter for fussy babies. If you're wondering how that was even legal, so was everyone else. Eventually, and the drugs were not the only hazard built into the system. There was also the disease. In 1780, the French government opened the vowerard hospital in Paris with a specific experimental purpose. Doctors wanted to test whether syphilytic infants could be cured by passing mercury through wet nurse milk. Mercury was too toxic to give directly to a baby. So instead, they dosed the wet nurses themselves with Van Sweeten's liquid and mercury pills, hoping the drug would transfer through their breast milk into the infected child. Many of the nurses died. The hospital closed in 1790 though the private practice of dosing nurses with mercury continued well after mammalary chankers the primary sypholytic lesion that forms on the nipple when an infected infant nurses were a recognized occupational hazard. CH's law established in 1837 held that a sypholytic baby could not infect its own biological mother but could and routinely did infect a healthy wet nurse. Joan Sherwood's 2010 study, Infection of the Innocence, documented 19th century lawsuits brought by wet nurses against the families and physicians who had knowingly concealed a child's syphilis before handing it over to nurse. And the timing of what happened next was almost too perfect. Because the same year that Curtis was testifying about his million bottle morphine operation, the editor of the British Medical Journal decided to run his own experiment, Ernest Hart published a five-part expose in 1868 titled Baby Farming and Baby Murder. His method was direct. He placed a fake advertisement in a newspaper posing as someone seeking a nurse for an unwanted infant. He received 333 responses. 333 women writing in to take custody of a baby. Many of them with no intention of keeping it alive. Hart series drove the passage of the Infant Life Protection Act of 1,872 which was strengthened after the Dire case in 1897 and consolidated into the Children Act of 1,98. In France, the physician Pierre Bodí and Senator Theophile Rousel drove the Rousel law of the 23rd of December 1874, which required the registration and inspection of every infant placed with a paid guardian anywhere in France. By the time of the First World War, French wet nursing mortality had dropped from over 30% to 15. The angel makers did not disappear because people became kinder. They disappeared because the law finally started counting the dead babies. But legislation alone did not kill the wet nursing trade. By the mid 1800s, a series of inventions were converging that would make the entire profession obsolete, and the clock on the oldest female labor market in human history had already started ticking. In 1845, a man named Elijah Pratt in New York patented the first rubber nipple for a baby bottle. It was made of black vulcanized rubber. It stank. It fell apart in hot water. And it started a revolution. Within two decades, manufacturers were selling banjo-shaped feeding bottles with long rubber tubes marketed under names like Mummy's Darling, The Little Cherub, The Princess, and the Alexandra. They were impossible to clean. The tubes collected bacteria, Mrs. Beaton, the famous domestic authority, advised that the nipple did not need washing for 2 or 3 weeks. Doctors gave these bottles their own names. The killer, the murderer, the murder bottle. They were sold well into the 1920s. But behind the disastrous early designs, the real breakthrough was happening in chemistry labs. In 1865, the German chemist von Liebig published a formula called supe fur sling and marketed libig soluble food for babies. The first product ever engineered to chemically replicate human breast milk. 2 years later in 1867, a Swiss merchant named Henri Nestle introduced fine lacti Nestle. He explained that his product was prepared entirely on Liebig's principles. only I reach the same goal by other means. By 1873, Nestle was selling half a million boxes a year. Gail Bordon's condensed milk patent from 1,856. And the demand created by the American Civil War made shelf stable milk a national product. and pasteurization applied to commercial milk by the 1880s finally eliminated the bacterial death trap of unrefrigerated cow's milk. The man who put all of this together into a public health campaign was Nathan Strauss, the co-owner of Macy's department store in New York. After his own children died and a healthylooking cow on his farm turned out to have tuberculosis, Strauss became obsessed with milk safety. He opened his first pasteurized milk depot at the East Third Street Pier in New York on the 1st of June 1893. His slogan was blunt. Stop the slaughter of babies. He called infant deaths permitted murder for which the responsibility must lie at the door of the agencies of government. Of 20,11 infants fed by his depots over 4 years, only six died. New York's child mortality rate fell from 126 to 74 per thousand in a decade. The wet nurse was no longer the only option and once she stopped being necessary, the profession collapsed fast. The Paris Bureau denies closed in 1876 in England. Wet nursing among the working classes faded by the early 1800s and among the wealthy by 1914. In the United States, it was effectively dead by the 1920s. In Rome, the Piaza Montinara, where women had gathered to sell their milk on the same ground as the ancient Columna Lakaria, was demolished in 1928 to make way for Mussolini's road projects. Nearly 2,000 years, same spot, gone. This is where the story takes a turn that nobody expected. Because the loudest voice calling for the end of wet nursing turned out to be one of history's greatest hypocrites. For 2,000 years, philosophers had been arguing about whether mothers should nurse their own children. Plutarch wrote that mothers ought to nurse their infants themselves because the goodwill of hired nurses was insincere and forced since they love for pay. Arasmus in 1526 had a character in one of his dialogues tell a new mother that she was only half a mother if she sent her baby to a nurse. Michelle Deontaine writing in the 1580s noted that all of his children had died at nurse except one. Leonor our only daughter who has escaped this misfortune has reached the age of six and more. Five of his six daughters died with country nurses. Montaigne himself had been sent at birth to a peasant family on his father's orders. Then came Jean Jacqu Rouso. In 1762 he published a meal, one of the most influential books on education ever written. In it, he declared, "Would you restore all men to their primary duties? Begin with the mothers. Let mothers dain to nurse their children. Morals will reform themselves." The book transformed elite European opinion almost overnight.
